title: Magnetic Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor
lead: A magnetic field pushes sideways on a charge that moves through it, and a charge in a wire cannot leave the wire, so whatever the field does to the charges it does to the wire as well. Adding the force on every carrier in a length of wire turns a law about single particles into a law about circuits: the force is the current times the length of wire in the field times the field strength times the sine of the angle between the current and the field, and its direction is given by the same right hand rule as before, with the thumb now laid along the current. The section ends with an application in which the conductor is not a wire at all but a fluid, and the force pumps it along a tube that has no moving part in it.
objectives: Describe the effects of a magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor.
Calculate the magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor.
summary_html: • The magnetic force on current-carrying conductors is given by $\kF = \kIcur l\kBmag\sin\theta,$ where $\kIcur$ is the current, $l$ is the length of a straight conductor in a uniform magnetic field $\kBmag$, and $\theta$ is the angle between $\kIcur$ and $\kBmag$. The force follows RHR-1 with the thumb in the direction of $\kIcur$.

figures.original_caption: The magnetic field exerts a force on a current-carrying wire in a direction given by the right hand rule 1 (the same direction as that on the individual moving charges). This force can easily be large enough to move the wire, since typical currents consist of very large numbers of moving charges.
The force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field is F = IlB sin θ. Its direction is given by RHR-1.

exercises.prompt: Draw a sketch of the situation in Figure 22.29 showing the direction of electrons carrying the current, and use RHR-1 to verify the direction of the force on the wire.

answer.solution: The conventional current comes out of the page toward you, so the electrons, which carry a negative charge, drift the other way, into the page. Apply RHR-1 to one of those electrons: its velocity is into the page and the field runs from the north pole to the south pole, across the wire, so the fingers lie along the field and the thumb points into the page, which puts the perpendicular to the palm downward. That is the force a positive charge moving into the page would feel, and the electron’s charge is negative, so the force on the electron is the opposite of it, upward. Every carrier in the wire is pushed upward, and because the carriers cannot leave the wire the wire is pushed upward too, which is the direction RHR-1 gives at once when the thumb is laid along the conventional current instead.

exercises.prompt: Verify that the direction of the force in an MHD drive, such as that in Figure 22.31, does not depend on the sign of the charges carrying the current across the fluid.

answer.solution: Take the positive carriers first. They drift the way the conventional current runs, across the duct from one electrode to the other, and RHR-1 with the thumb along that drift and the fingers along the field gives a force along the duct. Now take the negative carriers. They drift the opposite way, so the velocity in the force law reverses; but their charge is negative as well, so the force reverses a second time. Two reversals leave the direction as it was, and the negative carriers are pushed along the duct exactly as the positive ones are. That is why a fluid such as sea water, which carries both signs at once, is driven one way as a whole rather than being pulled apart, and why the pump works whichever sign happens to carry most of the current.

exercises.prompt: Why would a magnetohydrodynamic drive work better in ocean water than in fresh water? Also, why would superconducting magnets be desirable?

answer.solution: The force on the fluid is the current across the duct times the width of the duct times the field, so everything depends on getting a large current through the fluid. Ocean water is full of dissolved salt, which puts a great many ions into every cubic centimeter, and those ions are the charge carriers; fresh water has far fewer of them, so at the same voltage between the electrodes it carries a much smaller current and feels a much smaller force. Superconducting magnets are wanted for the other factor in the same product. A large field is what makes the force worth having, and an ordinary electromagnet strong enough to give it would dissipate a great deal of power as heat in its own windings, and would have to be cooled. A superconducting winding carries its current with no resistance, so it holds a strong field steadily without that loss, which matters especially in a submarine, where the power comes from the reactor and quietness is the point of the drive.

exercises.prompt: Which is more likely to interfere with compass readings, AC current in your refrigerator or DC current when you start your car? Explain.

answer.solution: The direct current that starts a car is the more likely of the two to move a compass needle. It is very large, some hundreds of amperes, and it runs steadily in one direction for the second or two the starter turns, so the field it makes is steady as well and holds the needle away from north for long enough to see. The alternating current in a refrigerator is smaller, and it reverses sixty times a second, so the field it makes reverses with it. A compass needle has far too much inertia to follow a field that changes that quickly, and what it feels is the average of the two directions, which is nothing at all. A steady field of a given size deflects a compass; a rapidly alternating one of the same size leaves it pointing north.

exercises.prompt: (a) A DC power line for a light-rail system carries 1000 A at an angle of $30.0^\circ$ to the Earth’s $\text{5.00}\times {\text{10}}^{-5}\;\text{-T}$ field. What is the force on a 100-m section of this line? (b) Discuss practical concerns this presents, if any.

answer.hint: The whole of the 100 m lies in the field, so use the force on a length of wire with the sine of 30.0°, which is one half.
answer.solution:
(a) 2.50 N
(b) This is about half a pound of force per 100 m of wire, which is much less than the weight of the wire itself. Therefore, it does not cause any special concerns.

exercises.prompt: A wire carrying a 30.0-A current passes between the poles of a strong magnet that is perpendicular to its field and experiences a 2.16-N force on the 4.00 cm of wire in the field. What is the average field strength?

answer.hint: Solve the force on a length of wire for the field, remembering that the wire lies across the field so the sine is 1, and that 4.00 cm is 0.0400 m.

exercises.prompt: (a) What is the angle between a wire carrying an 8.00-A current and the 1.20-T field it is in if 50.0 cm of the wire experiences a magnetic force of 2.40 N? (b) What is the force on the wire if it is rotated to make an angle of $90^\circ$ with the field?

parts.hint: Solve the force on a length of wire for the sine of the angle, and take the angle between zero and ninety degrees.
At ninety degrees the sine is 1, so the force is the whole of the current times the length times the field.

exercises.prompt: A wire oriented north-south carries current south. The wire is immersed in the Earths magnetic field, which is also oriented north-south (with a horizontal component pointing north). The Earths magnetic field also has a vertical component pointing down. What is the direction of the magnetic force felt by the wire?

answer.hint: The part of the field that lies along the wire does nothing, so only the vertical component of Earth’s field is left to push on the current. Lay the thumb south and the fingers down.
